# Preemption, the condo model, and checkpointing {#sec-preemption}

::: {.tldr}
MedicineBow is a **condo**: research groups buy `inv-*` nodes, and the rest of us borrow them
when idle. The catch — **the owner can reclaim their node at any moment, and your job is
automatically requeued** (killed and put back in line). Long jobs must therefore either run on
`non-investor` partitions *or* **checkpoint** so a requeue costs minutes, not days.
:::

## The condo model, plainly

A lot of MedicineBow's hardware was purchased by individual research groups. Those `inv-*`
partitions "belong" to their investors, who get top priority (QOS 110) on them. To keep the
machine busy, everyone else's jobs can **backfill** onto idle investor nodes — free capacity,
most of the time.

The deal has a string attached:

::: {.callout-warning}
## An investor can reclaim their node and requeue your job
If you land on investor hardware and the owner submits work, **your job is preempted** — Slurm
kills it and (by default here) **requeues** it: it goes back into the pending queue to start
over from the beginning when resources free up. Any progress not written to disk is lost.
This can happen minutes into a job or days in. For a long, un-checkpointed simulation, that's
potentially days of wasted compute.
:::

## Two ways to protect a long run

**1. Run where you can't be preempted.** Submit long production jobs to the non-preemptible
pool:

```bash
#SBATCH --partition=non-investor        # 110 CPU nodes, not reclaimable
# or non-investor-gpu for GPU work
```

This is the correct home for anything long that you haven't checkpointed. (The
`--constraint=non-investor` some docs mention **does not work** — it's a *partition*, not a
constraint. See @sec-partitions.)

**2. Checkpoint, so preemption is cheap.** If you *do* run on borrowable hardware (or list
several partitions for faster starts), make preemption survivable by saving state
periodically.

## Checkpointing {#sec-checkpointing}

A checkpoint is a periodic save of enough state to *resume* rather than *restart*. It protects
you from three things at once: preemption, node failures, and hitting your walltime limit. Any
job measured in days should checkpoint.

**The pattern:**

1. Every so often (every N iterations, or every ~30–60 min of wall time), write current state
   to a checkpoint file in `/gscratch` or `/project` — not `/lscratch`, which is wiped when
   the job ends (@sec-storage).
2. On startup, check for a checkpoint and **resume from it if present**, otherwise start fresh.
3. Write checkpoints atomically (write to a temp file, then rename) so a crash mid-write can't
   corrupt your only checkpoint. Keep the last one or two.

Many scientific codes have this built in — WRF has restart files, PyTorch has
`torch.save`/`load` for model+optimizer state, PETSc and Sundials have checkpoint hooks. Turn
these on and set the interval to your risk tolerance.

**Auto-resubmit on requeue.** Combine checkpointing with a self-resubmitting job so a preempted
or timed-out job comes back automatically:

```bash
#SBATCH --requeue                          # allow this job to be requeued
#SBATCH --open-mode=append                 # don't clobber the log on requeue
#SBATCH --signal=B:USR1@120                # send USR1 120s before the walltime kill

# resume from checkpoint if one exists
if [ -f state.ckpt ]; then
    ./simulate --restart state.ckpt
else
    ./simulate --fresh
fi
```

The `--signal` line asks Slurm to warn your script 120 seconds before it's killed for
walltime; trap that signal to flush a final checkpoint before you go.

## Requeue behavior worth knowing

- A requeued job keeps its **job ID** but starts its command **from the beginning** — Slurm
  doesn't magically resume your program; your *checkpoint* does.
- `--open-mode=append` stops the requeued run from overwriting the previous log.
- Check whether a job was requeued with `sacct -j <id> --format=JobID,State,Start,End` — you'll
  see multiple rows.

## The one-line policy

::: {.callout-important}
## If a job runs longer than a few hours, checkpoint it
Short jobs (minutes to an hour or two) can just be rerun if something goes wrong — don't
over-engineer them. But **any multi-hour or multi-day job should checkpoint**, and any long
production run should also prefer `non-investor`. The combination — non-preemptible partition
*and* checkpoints — is what lets big simulations finish reliably on a shared, condo-model
machine.
:::
